# Task: Add and remove pips in a row with the keyboard

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera; one world unit is ten pixels. It shows a thin grey rail named Rail. The program also defines Pip, a reusable description of one small sky-blue block (0.8 by 0.8 world units, #38bdf8) that takes its horizontal position x as an input and sits at (x, 0, 0). No Pip exists at the start: Pips are created and removed while the program runs.
Make the keyboard fill and empty a row of Pips:
- A press of the Space bar adds a Pip at the next free place: the n-th Pip that currently exists is at x = -6 + 2n, so the places are x = -4, -2, 0, 2 and 4, in that order. At most five Pips exist: a press of Space while five exist does nothing.
- A press of the Backspace key removes the most recently added Pip (the one furthest right); with no Pip it does nothing. A place that was emptied is free again.
- A press of the Enter key removes all Pips.
Every key press counts and takes effect in the order the presses were made, also when several keys are pressed in the same frame. A removed Pip leaves nothing behind in the picture. The rail, the definition of Pip, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Pip, Demo.Rail

- Only mtek.toml and the .mtek files under src/ can be changed.
- The project's tests are hidden and run after your edit. Do not delete, rename or hollow out a declaration to make an error go away: the declarations the task names must still exist and still do their job.
- Use only what the compiler context lists as supported. Features listed under notSupported do not exist in this compiler.
- When a diagnostic carries a suggestedEdit, it has been validated by the compiler; otherwise do not guess beyond what the message says.

messages.content:
# Task: Add and remove pips in a row with the keyboard

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera; one world unit is ten pixels. It shows a thin grey rail named Rail. The program also defines Pip, a reusable description of one small sky-blue block (0.8 by 0.8 world units, #38bdf8) that takes its horizontal position x as an input and sits at (x, 0, 0). No Pip exists at the start: Pips are created and removed while the program runs.
Make the keyboard fill and empty a row of Pips:
- A press of the Space bar adds a Pip at the next free place: the n-th Pip that currently exists is at x = -6 + 2n, so the places are x = -4, -2, 0, 2 and 4, in that order. At most five Pips exist: a press of Space while five exist does nothing.
- A press of the Backspace key removes the most recently added Pip (the one furthest right); with no Pip it does nothing. A place that was emptied is free again.
- A press of the Enter key removes all Pips.
Every key press counts and takes effect in the order the presses were made, also when several keys are pressed in the same frame. A removed Pip leaves nothing behind in the picture. The rail, the definition of Pip, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Pip, Demo.Rail

messages.content:
# Task: Add and remove pips in a row with the keyboard

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera; one world unit is ten pixels. It shows a thin grey rail named Rail. The program also defines Pip, a reusable description of one small sky-blue block (0.8 by 0.8 world units, #38bdf8) that takes its horizontal position x as an input and sits at (x, 0, 0). No Pip exists at the start: Pips are created and removed while the program runs.
Make the keyboard fill and empty a row of Pips:
- A press of the Space bar adds a Pip at the next free place: the n-th Pip that currently exists is at x = -6 + 2n, so the places are x = -4, -2, 0, 2 and 4, in that order. At most five Pips exist: a press of Space while five exist does nothing.
- A press of the Backspace key removes the most recently added Pip (the one furthest right); with no Pip it does nothing. A place that was emptied is free again.
- A press of the Enter key removes all Pips.
Every key press counts and takes effect in the order the presses were made, also when several keys are pressed in the same frame. A removed Pip leaves nothing behind in the picture. The rail, the definition of Pip, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Pip, Demo.Rail

messages.content:
# Task: A runner that Space starts and stops and that wraps around

Build a scene named Demo that looks and behaves as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #202020.
- One camera at (0, 0, 10) looking at the origin, with an orthographic projection whose visible height is 12.8 world units (near plane 0.1, far plane 1000); so one world unit is ten pixels.
- A thin dark grey track named Track: a box 12 wide, 0.2 high and 0.2 deep at (0, -1, 0), colour #404040.
- An orange block named Runner: a box 1 wide, 1 high and 0.5 deep, colour #f97316, starting at (-5, 0, 0). It starts stopped.
- A press of the Space bar toggles the Runner between stopped and moving. While it is moving it moves along +X at 4 world units per second of program time (program time is the sum of the frame durations the program is given; the distance covered in a frame is 4 times that frame's duration). While it is stopped it stays where it is, and starting it again continues from there.
- The Runner's x is kept in the range -6 <= x < 6: when moving takes it to 6 or beyond, 12 is subtracted, so it re-enters at the left.
All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting). Nothing else moves.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Runner, Demo.Track

messages.content:
# Task: A runner that Space starts and stops and that wraps around

Build a scene named Demo that looks and behaves as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #202020.
- One camera at (0, 0, 10) looking at the origin, with an orthographic projection whose visible height is 12.8 world units (near plane 0.1, far plane 1000); so one world unit is ten pixels.
- A thin dark grey track named Track: a box 12 wide, 0.2 high and 0.2 deep at (0, -1, 0), colour #404040.
- An orange block named Runner: a box 1 wide, 1 high and 0.5 deep, colour #f97316, starting at (-5, 0, 0). It starts stopped.
- A press of the Space bar toggles the Runner between stopped and moving. While it is moving it moves along +X at 4 world units per second of program time (program time is the sum of the frame durations the program is given; the distance covered in a frame is 4 times that frame's duration). While it is stopped it stays where it is, and starting it again continues from there.
- The Runner's x is kept in the range -6 <= x < 6: when moving takes it to 6 or beyond, 12 is subtracted, so it re-enters at the left.
All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting). Nothing else moves.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Runner, Demo.Track

messages.content:
# Task: A runner that Space starts and stops and that wraps around

Build a scene named Demo that looks and behaves as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #202020.
- One camera at (0, 0, 10) looking at the origin, with an orthographic projection whose visible height is 12.8 world units (near plane 0.1, far plane 1000); so one world unit is ten pixels.
- A thin dark grey track named Track: a box 12 wide, 0.2 high and 0.2 deep at (0, -1, 0), colour #404040.
- An orange block named Runner: a box 1 wide, 1 high and 0.5 deep, colour #f97316, starting at (-5, 0, 0). It starts stopped.
- A press of the Space bar toggles the Runner between stopped and moving. While it is moving it moves along +X at 4 world units per second of program time (program time is the sum of the frame durations the program is given; the distance covered in a frame is 4 times that frame's duration). While it is stopped it stays where it is, and starting it again continues from there.
- The Runner's x is kept in the range -6 <= x < 6: when moving takes it to 6 or beyond, 12 is subtracted, so it re-enters at the left.
All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting). Nothing else moves.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Runner, Demo.Track

messages.content:
# Task: A runner that Space starts and stops and that wraps around

Build a scene named Demo that looks and behaves as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #202020.
- One camera at (0, 0, 10) looking at the origin, with an orthographic projection whose visible height is 12.8 world units (near plane 0.1, far plane 1000); so one world unit is ten pixels.
- A thin dark grey track named Track: a box 12 wide, 0.2 high and 0.2 deep at (0, -1, 0), colour #404040.
- An orange block named Runner: a box 1 wide, 1 high and 0.5 deep, colour #f97316, starting at (-5, 0, 0). It starts stopped.
- A press of the Space bar toggles the Runner between stopped and moving. While it is moving it moves along +X at 4 world units per second of program time (program time is the sum of the frame durations the program is given; the distance covered in a frame is 4 times that frame's duration). While it is stopped it stays where it is, and starting it again continues from there.
- The Runner's x is kept in the range -6 <= x < 6: when moving takes it to 6 or beyond, 12 is subtracted, so it re-enters at the left.
All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting). Nothing else moves.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Runner, Demo.Track

# Task: A spring-loaded launcher: charge while Space is held, fire when it is released

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. One world unit is ten pixels. A yellow block named Stone (#ffd24a, 2 x 2 units) rests on a thin grey rail with its centre at x = -4. Above it a small block named Power shows a whole-number counter called power: the centre of Power is at x = -5.5 + power. power starts at 0, the scene already draws Power from it, and no key changes power yet.
Make the Space key a spring-loaded launcher:
- While Space is held down the Stone is orange (#ff7a1a); at every other time it is yellow (#ffd24a).
- While Space is held down, each press of the Up arrow key adds 1 to power, up to a maximum of 5. A press of Up while Space is not held does nothing.
- When Space is released the Stone is launched: it moves 2 world units to the right for every point of power, but its centre never goes beyond x = 5 (a launch that would take it further leaves it at x = 5). Then power goes back to 0. A launch with power 0 moves nothing.
- Pressing Space, or releasing Up, does nothing by itself: only the release of Space launches.
Every key press and every key release counts and is handled in the order in which it happened, also when several happen at the same moment (in the same frame). For example, pressing Space, pressing Up and releasing Space within one frame launches the Stone with power 1. Without any key event nothing changes. The rail, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Stone, Demo.Power, Demo.power

messages.content:
# Task: A spring-loaded launcher: charge while Space is held, fire when it is released

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. One world unit is ten pixels. A yellow block named Stone (#ffd24a, 2 x 2 units) rests on a thin grey rail with its centre at x = -4. Above it a small block named Power shows a whole-number counter called power: the centre of Power is at x = -5.5 + power. power starts at 0, the scene already draws Power from it, and no key changes power yet.
Make the Space key a spring-loaded launcher:
- While Space is held down the Stone is orange (#ff7a1a); at every other time it is yellow (#ffd24a).
- While Space is held down, each press of the Up arrow key adds 1 to power, up to a maximum of 5. A press of Up while Space is not held does nothing.
- When Space is released the Stone is launched: it moves 2 world units to the right for every point of power, but its centre never goes beyond x = 5 (a launch that would take it further leaves it at x = 5). Then power goes back to 0. A launch with power 0 moves nothing.
- Pressing Space, or releasing Up, does nothing by itself: only the release of Space launches.
Every key press and every key release counts and is handled in the order in which it happened, also when several happen at the same moment (in the same frame). For example, pressing Space, pressing Up and releasing Space within one frame launches the Stone with power 1. Without any key event nothing changes. The rail, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Stone, Demo.Power, Demo.power

# Task: A spring-loaded launcher: charge while Space is held, fire when it is released

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. One world unit is ten pixels. A yellow block named Stone (#ffd24a, 2 x 2 units) rests on a thin grey rail with its centre at x = -4. Above it a small block named Power shows a whole-number counter called power: the centre of Power is at x = -5.5 + power. power starts at 0, the scene already draws Power from it, and no key changes power yet.
Make the Space key a spring-loaded launcher:
- While Space is held down the Stone is orange (#ff7a1a); at every other time it is yellow (#ffd24a).
- While Space is held down, each press of the Up arrow key adds 1 to power, up to a maximum of 5. A press of Up while Space is not held does nothing.
- When Space is released the Stone is launched: it moves 2 world units to the right for every point of power, but its centre never goes beyond x = 5 (a launch that would take it further leaves it at x = 5). Then power goes back to 0. A launch with power 0 moves nothing.
- Pressing Space, or releasing Up, does nothing by itself: only the release of Space launches.
Every key press and every key release counts and is handled in the order in which it happened, also when several happen at the same moment (in the same frame). For example, pressing Space, pressing Up and releasing Space within one frame launches the Stone with power 1. Without any key event nothing changes. The rail, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Stone, Demo.Power, Demo.power

Above it a small block named Power shows a whole-number counter called power: the centre of Power is at x = -5.5 + power. power starts at 0, the scene already draws Power from it, and no key changes power yet.
Make the Space key a spring-loaded launcher:
- While Space is held down the Stone is orange (#ff7a1a); at every other time it is yellow (#ffd24a).
- While Space is held down, each press of the Up arrow key adds 1 to power, up to a maximum of 5. A press of Up while Space is not held does nothing.
- When Space is released the Stone is launched: it moves 2 world units to the right for every point of power, but its centre never goes beyond x = 5 (a launch that would take it further leaves it at x = 5). Then power goes back to 0. A launch with power 0 moves nothing.
- Pressing Space, or releasing Up, does nothing by itself: only the release of Space launches.
Every key press and every key release counts and is handled in the order in which it happened, also when several happen at the same moment (in the same frame). For example, pressing Space, pressing Up and releasing Space within one frame launches the Stone with power 1. Without any key event nothing changes. The rail, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

messages.content:
# Task: Fly a ship with the arrow keys: it moves in every frame a key is held

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. One world unit is ten pixels. A blue square block named Ship (#38bdf8, 2 x 2 units) is at the centre, x = 0 and y = 0, on a dark grey square named Field (10 x 10 units, centred on the origin).
Make the arrow keys fly the Ship:
- While the Right arrow key is held down the Ship moves along +X at 8 world units per second of program time: in every frame in which the key is held it moves 8 times that frame's duration. Left moves it along -X, Up along +Y and Down along -Y in the same way. Program time is the sum of the frame durations the program is given, and frame durations vary.
- Keys that are held at the same time all act at the same time: Right and Up together move the Ship diagonally, 8 units per second along each of the two axes; two opposite keys held together cancel each other out.
- A key counts as held in the frame in which its press is handled and in every later frame up to, but not including, the frame in which its release is handled. A key that is pressed and released again within the same frame is not held in any frame, so it moves nothing.
- After every frame the centre of the Ship is limited to x and y between -4 and 4, each axis on its own, so the Ship stays inside the Field.
Without a held key nothing moves. The Field, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Ship, Demo.Field

messages.content:
# Task: Fly a ship with the arrow keys: it moves in every frame a key is held

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. One world unit is ten pixels. A blue square block named Ship (#38bdf8, 2 x 2 units) is at the centre, x = 0 and y = 0, on a dark grey square named Field (10 x 10 units, centred on the origin).
Make the arrow keys fly the Ship:
- While the Right arrow key is held down the Ship moves along +X at 8 world units per second of program time: in every frame in which the key is held it moves 8 times that frame's duration. Left moves it along -X, Up along +Y and Down along -Y in the same way. Program time is the sum of the frame durations the program is given, and frame durations vary.
- Keys that are held at the same time all act at the same time: Right and Up together move the Ship diagonally, 8 units per second along each of the two axes; two opposite keys held together cancel each other out.
- A key counts as held in the frame in which its press is handled and in every later frame up to, but not including, the frame in which its release is handled. A key that is pressed and released again within the same frame is not held in any frame, so it moves nothing.
- After every frame the centre of the Ship is limited to x and y between -4 and 4, each axis on its own, so the Ship stays inside the Field.
Without a held key nothing moves. The Field, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Ship, Demo.Field

# Task: Two clocks: a block that moves per fixed tick and a block that moves per frame time

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. One world unit is ten pixels. Two blocks of 1 x 1 units stand at the left with their centres at x = -5.5: a red block named Ticker (#ef4444) at y = 3 and a cyan block named Glider (#38bdf8) at y = -3. Neither moves yet.
The program has two clocks:
- Frames. Every frame has a duration, the time since the previous frame; a duration longer than 0.1 s counts as 0.1 s. Program time is the sum of the counted durations.
- Fixed steps. The simulation runs in steps of exactly 1/60 s of program time, one tick per step. In each frame the counted duration is added to whatever is left over from earlier frames, and every whole 1/60 s in that sum is one tick, run in order within that frame, but at most 4 ticks run in one frame. Whole steps beyond the fourth are dropped: they are never run later. What is less than one step is kept for the next frame. For example, starting with nothing left over, a frame of 0.04 s (2.4 steps) runs 2 ticks and keeps 0.4 of a step.
Make both blocks move to the right:
- The Ticker moves 0.1 world unit (one pixel) on every tick.
- The Glider moves 6 world units per second of program time: in every frame it moves 6 times that frame's counted duration.
Neither block moves in any other way. The camera and everything else stay as they are.

messages.content:
# Task: Two clocks: a block that moves per fixed tick and a block that moves per frame time

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. One world unit is ten pixels. Two blocks of 1 x 1 units stand at the left with their centres at x = -5.5: a red block named Ticker (#ef4444) at y = 3 and a cyan block named Glider (#38bdf8) at y = -3. Neither moves yet.
The program has two clocks:
- Frames. Every frame has a duration, the time since the previous frame; a duration longer than 0.1 s counts as 0.1 s. Program time is the sum of the counted durations.
- Fixed steps. The simulation runs in steps of exactly 1/60 s of program time, one tick per step. In each frame the counted duration is added to whatever is left over from earlier frames, and every whole 1/60 s in that sum is one tick, run in order within that frame, but at most 4 ticks run in one frame. Whole steps beyond the fourth are dropped: they are never run later. What is less than one step is kept for the next frame. For example, starting with nothing left over, a frame of 0.04 s (2.4 steps) runs 2 ticks and keeps 0.4 of a step.
Make both blocks move to the right:
- The Ticker moves 0.1 world unit (one pixel) on every tick.
- The Glider moves 6 world units per second of program time: in every frame it moves 6 times that frame's counted duration.
Neither block moves in any other way. The camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Ticker, Demo.Glider

# Task: Two clocks: a block that moves per fixed tick and a block that moves per frame time

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. One world unit is ten pixels. Two blocks of 1 x 1 units stand at the left with their centres at x = -5.5: a red block named Ticker (#ef4444) at y = 3 and a cyan block named Glider (#38bdf8) at y = -3. Neither moves yet.
The program has two clocks:
- Frames. Every frame has a duration, the time since the previous frame; a duration longer than 0.1 s counts as 0.1 s. Program time is the sum of the counted durations.
- Fixed steps. The simulation runs in steps of exactly 1/60 s of program time, one tick per step. In each frame the counted duration is added to whatever is left over from earlier frames, and every whole 1/60 s in that sum is one tick, run in order within that frame, but at most 4 ticks run in one frame. Whole steps beyond the fourth are dropped: they are never run later. What is less than one step is kept for the next frame. For example, starting with nothing left over, a frame of 0.04 s (2.4 steps) runs 2 ticks and keeps 0.4 of a step.
Make both blocks move to the right:
- The Ticker moves 0.1 world unit (one pixel) on every tick.
- The Glider moves 6 world units per second of program time: in every frame it moves 6 times that frame's counted duration.
Neither block moves in any other way. The camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Ticker, Demo.Glider

messages.content:
# Task: Fix an off-by-one in the loop that places a row of markers

The project is meant to build up rows of markers: every press of Space places one new row, and it does not place the rows correctly. Repair it without removing or renaming anything.
Intended behaviour: clear colour #202020; one camera at (0, 0, 8) looking at the origin; a box named Rail, 8 x 0.4 x 1, at (0, -3, 0) with the flat colour #475569, which is always there. A marker is a box with edge length 0.8 and the flat colour #facc15. Each press of Space places one new row of exactly five markers: their x are -3, -1.5, 0, 1.5 and 3 (centred on x = 0, 1.5 apart) and their z is 0. The first row is at y = 2.0 and every further row is 2.5 lower than the previous one; the markers of earlier rows stay where they are. Before the first press there are no markers. All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Rail, Marker

# Task: Repair a turret that turns by the wrong amount and to the wrong side

The project is meant to show a turret that turns when Space is pressed, and the turret does not end up where it should. Repair it without removing anything.
Intended scene: clear colour #202020; one camera at (0, 0, 8) looking at the origin; a cube named Turret with edge length 2 at the origin, flat colour #6b5cff; a cube named Barrel with edge length 0.8, flat colour #f59e0b, attached to the Turret as its child at the local position (0, 0, 2.2), so that at the start it is between the turret and the camera. All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting).
Intended behaviour: every press of Space turns the Turret by a further 30 degrees about the vertical axis (Y), to the right as seen from the camera: the barrel swings from the camera toward the right-hand side of the picture, so that after three presses it is at world (2.2, 0, 0) and after four it is at (1.905, 0, -1.1). The program keeps the heading, which grows by one step with each press, in a variable named heading.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Turret, Demo.Turret.Barrel, Demo.heading

response.text:
Looking at this task, I need to understand what's wrong with the turret rotation.

The intended behavior is:
- Each Space press rotates the turret 30 degrees to the right (as seen from camera)
- After 3 presses, barrel should be at world (2.2, 0, 0)
- After 4 presses, barrel should be at (1.905, 0, -1.1)

Currently, the code does:
```
heading += STEP_DEGREES;
Turret.rotation = quat.axis_angle(vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), -heading);
```

Let me analyze the math:
- The barrel starts at local position (0, 0, 2.2), pointing toward +Z (toward camera)
- "To the right as seen from camera" means rotating around Y-axis in the positive direction (counterclockwise when looking down the Y axis from above)
- After 1 press: heading = 30, rotation angle = -30 degrees
- After 3 presses: heading = 90, rotation angle = -90 degrees

If we rotate the local +Z direction by -90 degrees around Y, we get -X direction (pointing left), which gives world position (-2.2, 0, 0). But we want (2.2, 0, 0) - pointing right.

The issue is the negative sign. We should rotate positively (to the right), not negatively (to the left).

Additionally, we need to convert degrees to radians for `quat.axis_angle`, which expects radians.

Let me verify:
- Press 1: heading=30°, rotate by radians(30)° ≈ 0.524 rad → barrel at (2.2*sin(30°), 0, 2.2*cos(30°)) ≈ (1.1, 0, 1.905) 
- Press 3: heading=90°, rotate by radians(90)° = π/2 → barrel at (2.2, 0, 0) ✓
- Press 4: heading=120°, rotate by radians(120)° → barrel at (2.2*sin(120°), 0, 2.2*cos(120°)) = (1.905, 0, -1.1) ✓

So the fix is to use positive heading (no negation) and convert to radians.

<<<FILE src/main.mtek
<<<SEARCH
    on key_down(Key.Space) {
        heading += STEP_DEGREES;
        Turret.rotation = quat.axis_angle(vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), -heading);
    }
===
    on key_down(Key.Space) {
        heading += STEP_DEGREES;
        Turret.rotation = quat.axis_angle(vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), radians(heading));
    }
>>>REPLACE

const MAX_COUNT: i32 = 5;

scene Demo {
    clear_color: #202020;
    // How many pips are lit, from 0 to MAX_COUNT.
    state count: i32 = 0;

    camera Main {
        position: vec3(0.0, 0.0, 8.0);
        target: vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0);
    }

    entity Pip1 {
        position: vec3(-3.0, -2.0, 0.0);
        visible: bind(count >= 1);
        mesh: Box { size: vec3(0.7, 0.7, 0.7) };
        material: Unlit { color: #22c55e };
    }

    entity Pip2 {
        position: vec3(-1.5, -2.0, 0.0);
        visible: bind(count >= 2);
        mesh: Box { size: vec3(0.7, 0.7, 0.7) };
        material: Unlit { color: #22c55e };
    }

    entity Pip3 {
        position: vec3(0.0, -2.0, 0.0);
        visible: bind(count >= 3);
        mesh: Box { size: vec3(0.7, 0.7, 0.7) };
        material: Unlit { color: #22c55e };
    }

    entity Pip4 {
        position: vec3(1.5, -2.0, 0.0);
        visible: bind(count >= 4);
        mesh: Box { size: vec3(0.7, 0.7, 0.7) };
        material: Unlit { color: #22c55e };
    }

    entity Pip5 {
        position: vec3(3.0, -2.0, 0.0);
        visible: bind(count >= 5);
        mesh: Box { size: vec3(0.7, 0.7, 0.7) };
        material: Unlit { color: #22c55e };

    on key_down(Key.Space) {

- The clear (background) colour is #202020.

- A blue sphere named Ball at (2, 0, 0), that is to the right of the box as seen from the camera: colour #3b82f6, radius 0.5.

messages.content:
# Task: A tilted amber bar with a red ball at its end

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #101820.
- One camera at (0, 0, 8) looking at the origin, with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.8 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 100).
- An amber box named Bar centred at the origin: colour #f59e0b, edge length 4.0 along its own x axis, 1.0 along its own y axis and 0.5 along its own z axis. It is rotated about the world Z axis by 0.9272952 radians, counter-clockwise as seen from the camera (the angle whose cosine is 0.6 and whose sine is 0.8), so that its own x axis points along (0.6, 0.8, 0).
- A red sphere named Tip at (1.2, 1.6, 0), which is the middle of the end face of the bar that lies along its own +x axis: colour #ef4444, radius 0.6.
All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Bar, Demo.Tip

messages.content:
# Task: A two-segment arm built as a hierarchy of nodes

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #14161c.
- One camera at (0, 0, 9) looking at the origin, with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.8 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- A grey box named Base at (-2.5, -1.5, 0): colour #64748b, edge length 1.2.
- An arm made of nodes in a hierarchy. Every position, rotation and scale below is given relative to the node's PARENT, so a child moves, turns and scales with its parent. Rotations are counter-clockwise about the Z axis as seen from the camera, in radians.
  - Arm: a node with no shape at (-2.5, -1.5, 0), rotated by 0.6435011 (cosine 0.8, sine 0.6), scale 1. Its children:
    - Upper: a box named Upper at (2, 0, 0) in the Arm's frame, colour #3b82f6, edge lengths 4.0 along its own x axis, 0.8 along y and 0.6 along z.
    - Elbow: a node with no shape at (4, 0, 0) in the Arm's frame, rotated by -1.287002, uniform scale 0.75. Its children:
      - Fore: a box named Fore at (1.5, 0, 0) in the Elbow's frame, colour #22c55e, edge lengths 3.0 x 0.7 x 0.5 (before the Elbow's scale applies).
      - Hand: a sphere named Hand at (3, 0, 0) in the Elbow's frame, colour #f43f5e, radius 0.6 (before the Elbow's scale applies).
All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Base, Demo.Arm, Demo.Arm.Upper, Demo.Arm.Elbow, Demo.Arm.Elbow.Fore, Demo.Arm.Elbow.Hand

messages.content:
# Task: A two-segment arm built as a hierarchy of nodes

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #14161c.
- One camera at (0, 0, 9) looking at the origin, with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.8 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- A grey box named Base at (-2.5, -1.5, 0): colour #64748b, edge length 1.2.
- An arm made of nodes in a hierarchy. Every position, rotation and scale below is given relative to the node's PARENT, so a child moves, turns and scales with its parent. Rotations are counter-clockwise about the Z axis as seen from the camera, in radians.
  - Arm: a node with no shape at (-2.5, -1.5, 0), rotated by 0.6435011 (cosine 0.8, sine 0.6), scale 1. Its children:
    - Upper: a box named Upper at (2, 0, 0) in the Arm's frame, colour #3b82f6, edge lengths 4.0 along its own x axis, 0.8 along y and 0.6 along z.
    - Elbow: a node with no shape at (4, 0, 0) in the Arm's frame, rotated by -1.287002, uniform scale 0.75. Its children:
      - Fore: a box named Fore at (1.5, 0, 0) in the Elbow's frame, colour #22c55e, edge lengths 3.0 x 0.7 x 0.5 (before the Elbow's scale applies).
      - Hand: a sphere named Hand at (3, 0, 0) in the Elbow's frame, colour #f43f5e, radius 0.6 (before the Elbow's scale applies).
All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Base, Demo.Arm, Demo.Arm.Upper, Demo.Arm.Elbow, Demo.Arm.Elbow.Fore, Demo.Arm.Elbow.Hand

# Task: Three solids on a floor seen from an off-axis camera

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #9db4cc.
- One camera at (5, 4, 9) looking at the point (0, 1, 0), with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.7 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- A flat square floor named Floor: 12 x 12 units, lying in the plane y = 0 and centred on the origin, colour #4b5563. It is a one-sided surface that faces up (+Y); it is not drawn when seen from below.
- Three solids stand on the floor:
  - Tower: a box named Tower, colour #2563eb, 1.5 wide (x), 3.0 tall (y) and 1.5 deep (z), centred at (0, 1.5, 0).
  - Block: a box named Block, colour #dc2626, 2.0 wide (x), 1.0 tall (y) and 2.0 deep (z), centred at (1.5, 0.5, 1.8).
  - Ball: a sphere named Ball, colour #eab308, radius 0.8, centred at (-1.6, 0.8, 1.2).
All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting). Solids nearer to the camera hide what is behind them.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Floor, Demo.Tower, Demo.Block, Demo.Ball

# Task: Three solids on a floor seen from an off-axis camera

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #9db4cc.
- One camera at (5, 4, 9) looking at the point (0, 1, 0), with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.7 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- A flat square floor named Floor: 12 x 12 units, lying in the plane y = 0 and centred on the origin, colour #4b5563. It is a one-sided surface that faces up (+Y); it is not drawn when seen from below.
- Three solids stand on the floor:
  - Tower: a box named Tower, colour #2563eb, 1.5 wide (x), 3.0 tall (y) and 1.5 deep (z), centred at (0, 1.5, 0).
  - Block: a box named Block, colour #dc2626, 2.0 wide (x), 1.0 tall (y) and 2.0 deep (z), centred at (1.5, 0.5, 1.8).
  - Ball: a sphere named Ball, colour #eab308, radius 0.8, centred at (-1.6, 0.8, 1.2).
All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting). Solids nearer to the camera hide what is behind them.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Floor, Demo.Tower, Demo.Block, Demo.Ball

# Task: Switch to an orthographic camera, move the crate and sink a dome into the floor

The scene Demo shows a floor and a crate seen by a perspective camera. Change it so that it renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour stays #1a1d23.
- The camera becomes an orthographic one (parallel projection, no perspective foreshortening) at (0, 6, 6), looking at the origin. It shows a world height of 8 units and, because the picture is square, a world width of 8 units; near plane 0.1, far plane 100.
- The floor Floor stays as it is: a 7 x 7 one-sided surface facing up (+Y), lying in the plane y = 0, centred on the origin, colour #3f4a5a.
- The crate Crate keeps its size and colour and moves to (2, 0.75, -1).
- A new sphere named Dome, colour #38bdf8, radius 1.2, centred at (-1.5, 0, 1). Half of it is below the floor and is hidden by it.
All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting). Do not remove anything that already exists, except what the changes above replace.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Floor, Demo.Crate

messages.content:
# Task: A cube and a floor lit by one directional light and an ambient term

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #0b0d12.
- One camera at (2.5, 2.5, 5) looking at the origin, with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.9 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- Both solids use a physically based material of the metallic-roughness kind, non-metallic (metalness 0), so they show a diffuse colour and a weak specular highlight:
  - A box named Cube centred at the origin, edge length 2.0, base colour #c8a27a, roughness 0.8.
  - A flat square named Floor, 10 x 10 units, one-sided, facing up (+Y), lying in the plane y = -1 and centred at (0, -1, 0), base colour #8a929c, roughness 0.9.
- One white directional light named Sun that travels in the direction (0, -0.6, -0.8) (that is, down and away from the camera). Its strength is calibrated so that a perfectly matte (Lambertian) white surface whose normal points straight at the light renders as exactly white; a surface at an angle to the light receives proportionally less (the cosine of the angle).
- A white ambient light of 10% of that strength: it adds, to every surface and regardless of its orientation, 10% of the surface's own diffuse colour.
There are no shadows and no tone mapping: values above full brightness are simply clipped. The expected pixels were computed with the standard model (Lambertian diffuse plus a GGX specular term with Schlick Fresnel) and are checked with a tolerance of 6 per colour channel, which covers the small differences between implementations of that model (the shading of a tessellated sphere, rounding).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Sun, Demo.Floor, Demo.Cube

messages.content:
# Task: A cube and a floor lit by one directional light and an ambient term

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #0b0d12.
- One camera at (2.5, 2.5, 5) looking at the origin, with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.9 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- Both solids use a physically based material of the metallic-roughness kind, non-metallic (metalness 0), so they show a diffuse colour and a weak specular highlight:
  - A box named Cube centred at the origin, edge length 2.0, base colour #c8a27a, roughness 0.8.
  - A flat square named Floor, 10 x 10 units, one-sided, facing up (+Y), lying in the plane y = -1 and centred at (0, -1, 0), base colour #8a929c, roughness 0.9.
- One white directional light named Sun that travels in the direction (0, -0.6, -0.8) (that is, down and away from the camera). Its strength is calibrated so that a perfectly matte (Lambertian) white surface whose normal points straight at the light renders as exactly white; a surface at an angle to the light receives proportionally less (the cosine of the angle).
- A white ambient light of 10% of that strength: it adds, to every surface and regardless of its orientation, 10% of the surface's own diffuse colour.
There are no shadows and no tone mapping: values above full brightness are simply clipped. The expected pixels were computed with the standard model (Lambertian diffuse plus a GGX specular term with Schlick Fresnel) and are checked with a tolerance of 6 per colour channel, which covers the small differences between implementations of that model (the shading of a tessellated sphere, rounding).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Sun, Demo.Floor, Demo.Cube

messages.content:
# Task: A cube and a floor lit by one directional light and an ambient term

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #0b0d12.
- One camera at (2.5, 2.5, 5) looking at the origin, with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.9 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- Both solids use a physically based material of the metallic-roughness kind, non-metallic (metalness 0), so they show a diffuse colour and a weak specular highlight:
  - A box named Cube centred at the origin, edge length 2.0, base colour #c8a27a, roughness 0.8.
  - A flat square named Floor, 10 x 10 units, one-sided, facing up (+Y), lying in the plane y = -1 and centred at (0, -1, 0), base colour #8a929c, roughness 0.9.
- One white directional light named Sun that travels in the direction (0, -0.6, -0.8) (that is, down and away from the camera). Its strength is calibrated so that a perfectly matte (Lambertian) white surface whose normal points straight at the light renders as exactly white; a surface at an angle to the light receives proportionally less (the cosine of the angle).
- A white ambient light of 10% of that strength: it adds, to every surface and regardless of its orientation, 10% of the surface's own diffuse colour.
There are no shadows and no tone mapping: values above full brightness are simply clipped. The expected pixels were computed with the standard model (Lambertian diffuse plus a GGX specular term with Schlick Fresnel) and are checked with a tolerance of 6 per colour channel, which covers the small differences between implementations of that model (the shading of a tessellated sphere, rounding).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Sun, Demo.Floor, Demo.Cube

messages.content:
# Task: A cube and a floor lit by one directional light and an ambient term

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #0b0d12.
- One camera at (2.5, 2.5, 5) looking at the origin, with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.9 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- Both solids use a physically based material of the metallic-roughness kind, non-metallic (metalness 0), so they show a diffuse colour and a weak specular highlight:
  - A box named Cube centred at the origin, edge length 2.0, base colour #c8a27a, roughness 0.8.
  - A flat square named Floor, 10 x 10 units, one-sided, facing up (+Y), lying in the plane y = -1 and centred at (0, -1, 0), base colour #8a929c, roughness 0.9.
- One white directional light named Sun that travels in the direction (0, -0.6, -0.8) (that is, down and away from the camera). Its strength is calibrated so that a perfectly matte (Lambertian) white surface whose normal points straight at the light renders as exactly white; a surface at an angle to the light receives proportionally less (the cosine of the angle).
- A white ambient light of 10% of that strength: it adds, to every surface and regardless of its orientation, 10% of the surface's own diffuse colour.
There are no shadows and no tone mapping: values above full brightness are simply clipped. The expected pixels were computed with the standard model (Lambertian diffuse plus a GGX specular term with Schlick Fresnel) and are checked with a tolerance of 6 per colour channel, which covers the small differences between implementations of that model (the shading of a tessellated sphere, rounding).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Sun, Demo.Floor, Demo.Cube

messages.content:
# Task: A red ball on a floor lit by one point light

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #10131a.
- One camera at (0, 3, 8) looking at the point (0, 0.5, 0), with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.8 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- Both solids use a physically based material of the metallic-roughness kind, non-metallic (metalness 0), so they show a diffuse colour and a weak specular highlight:
  - A sphere named Ball centred at (0, 1, 0), radius 1.0, base colour #e11d48, roughness 0.7.
  - A flat square named Floor, 14 x 14 units, one-sided, facing up (+Y), lying in the plane y = 0 and centred on the origin, base colour #9aa5b1, roughness 0.9.
- One white point light named Lamp at (1.5, 3, 2.5) that shines equally in all directions, with no range limit. Its illumination falls off with the inverse square of the distance from the lamp, and its strength is calibrated so that a perfectly matte (Lambertian) white surface that is 3 units from the lamp and whose normal points straight at it renders as exactly white; a surface at an angle to the light receives proportionally less (the cosine of the angle).
- A white ambient light of 5% of that strength: it adds, to every surface and regardless of its orientation, 5% of the surface's own diffuse colour.
There are no shadows and no tone mapping: values above full brightness are simply clipped. The expected pixels were computed with the standard model (Lambertian diffuse plus a GGX specular term with Schlick Fresnel) and are checked with a tolerance of 6 per colour channel, which covers the small differences between implementations of that model (the shading of a tessellated sphere, rounding).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Lamp, Demo.Floor, Demo.Ball

messages.content:
# Task: A red ball on a floor lit by one point light

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #10131a.
- One camera at (0, 3, 8) looking at the point (0, 0.5, 0), with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.8 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- Both solids use a physically based material of the metallic-roughness kind, non-metallic (metalness 0), so they show a diffuse colour and a weak specular highlight:
  - A sphere named Ball centred at (0, 1, 0), radius 1.0, base colour #e11d48, roughness 0.7.
  - A flat square named Floor, 14 x 14 units, one-sided, facing up (+Y), lying in the plane y = 0 and centred on the origin, base colour #9aa5b1, roughness 0.9.
- One white point light named Lamp at (1.5, 3, 2.5) that shines equally in all directions, with no range limit. Its illumination falls off with the inverse square of the distance from the lamp, and its strength is calibrated so that a perfectly matte (Lambertian) white surface that is 3 units from the lamp and whose normal points straight at it renders as exactly white; a surface at an angle to the light receives proportionally less (the cosine of the angle).
- A white ambient light of 5% of that strength: it adds, to every surface and regardless of its orientation, 5% of the surface's own diffuse colour.
There are no shadows and no tone mapping: values above full brightness are simply clipped. The expected pixels were computed with the standard model (Lambertian diffuse plus a GGX specular term with Schlick Fresnel) and are checked with a tolerance of 6 per colour channel, which covers the small differences between implementations of that model (the shading of a tessellated sphere, rounding).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Lamp, Demo.Floor, Demo.Ball

messages.content:
# Task: A red ball on a floor lit by one point light

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #10131a.
- One camera at (0, 3, 8) looking at the point (0, 0.5, 0), with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.8 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- Both solids use a physically based material of the metallic-roughness kind, non-metallic (metalness 0), so they show a diffuse colour and a weak specular highlight:
  - A sphere named Ball centred at (0, 1, 0), radius 1.0, base colour #e11d48, roughness 0.7.
  - A flat square named Floor, 14 x 14 units, one-sided, facing up (+Y), lying in the plane y = 0 and centred on the origin, base colour #9aa5b1, roughness 0.9.
- One white point light named Lamp at (1.5, 3, 2.5) that shines equally in all directions, with no range limit. Its illumination falls off with the inverse square of the distance from the lamp, and its strength is calibrated so that a perfectly matte (Lambertian) white surface that is 3 units from the lamp and whose normal points straight at it renders as exactly white; a surface at an angle to the light receives proportionally less (the cosine of the angle).
- A white ambient light of 5% of that strength: it adds, to every surface and regardless of its orientation, 5% of the surface's own diffuse colour.
There are no shadows and no tone mapping: values above full brightness are simply clipped. The expected pixels were computed with the standard model (Lambertian diffuse plus a GGX specular term with Schlick Fresnel) and are checked with a tolerance of 6 per colour channel, which covers the small differences between implementations of that model (the shading of a tessellated sphere, rounding).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Lamp, Demo.Floor, Demo.Ball

messages.content:
# Task: A red ball on a floor lit by one point light

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #10131a.
- One camera at (0, 3, 8) looking at the point (0, 0.5, 0), with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.8 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- Both solids use a physically based material of the metallic-roughness kind, non-metallic (metalness 0), so they show a diffuse colour and a weak specular highlight:
  - A sphere named Ball centred at (0, 1, 0), radius 1.0, base colour #e11d48, roughness 0.7.
  - A flat square named Floor, 14 x 14 units, one-sided, facing up (+Y), lying in the plane y = 0 and centred on the origin, base colour #9aa5b1, roughness 0.9.
- One white point light named Lamp at (1.5, 3, 2.5) that shines equally in all directions, with no range limit. Its illumination falls off with the inverse square of the distance from the lamp, and its strength is calibrated so that a perfectly matte (Lambertian) white surface that is 3 units from the lamp and whose normal points straight at it renders as exactly white; a surface at an angle to the light receives proportionally less (the cosine of the angle).
- A white ambient light of 5% of that strength: it adds, to every surface and regardless of its orientation, 5% of the surface's own diffuse colour.
There are no shadows and no tone mapping: values above full brightness are simply clipped. The expected pixels were computed with the standard model (Lambertian diffuse plus a GGX specular term with Schlick Fresnel) and are checked with a tolerance of 6 per colour channel, which covers the small differences between implementations of that model (the shading of a tessellated sphere, rounding).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Lamp, Demo.Floor, Demo.Ball

messages.content:
# Task: Near and far clipping planes and a hidden object

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #1e293b.
- One camera at (0, 0, 10) looking at the origin, with a perspective projection: vertical field of view 0.9 radians, near plane 4.0, far plane 12.0. The depth of a point is its distance from the camera measured along the viewing direction, so the camera shows only what lies at a depth between 4 and 12; what is nearer than 4 or farther than 12 is cut off.
- Six boxes, all with flat colours (no lighting), each with its own name. Edge length 2.0 in every direction unless stated:
  - Mid at (0, 0, 0): colour #ef4444.
  - Slab at (-2.5, 0, 5.5): colour #22c55e.
  - Far at (3.2, 0, -4): colour #3b82f6, edge length 3.0.
  - Behind at (0, 0, 14): colour #ec4899.
  - Ghost at (3, 0, 2): colour #facc15. It exists in the scene but is hidden: it must not be drawn.
  - Rim at (3.2, -2.2, 0): colour #a855f7, edge lengths 2.0 (x), 2.0 (y) and 5.0 (z).
Nothing special has to be programmed for the clipping: it is what the camera's near and far planes do to ordinary solid boxes. As usual for solid surfaces, only the outside of a box is drawn (a face seen from behind is not drawn), so where a near or far plane cuts a box the part that is cut off simply is not there and the box is not filled in.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Mid, Demo.Slab, Demo.Far, Demo.Behind, Demo.Ghost, Demo.Rim

# Task: Near and far clipping planes and a hidden object

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #1e293b.
- One camera at (0, 0, 10) looking at the origin, with a perspective projection: vertical field of view 0.9 radians, near plane 4.0, far plane 12.0. The depth of a point is its distance from the camera measured along the viewing direction, so the camera shows only what lies at a depth between 4 and 12; what is nearer than 4 or farther than 12 is cut off.
- Six boxes, all with flat colours (no lighting), each with its own name. Edge length 2.0 in every direction unless stated:
  - Mid at (0, 0, 0): colour #ef4444.
  - Slab at (-2.5, 0, 5.5): colour #22c55e.
  - Far at (3.2, 0, -4): colour #3b82f6, edge length 3.0.
  - Behind at (0, 0, 14): colour #ec4899.
  - Ghost at (3, 0, 2): colour #facc15. It exists in the scene but is hidden: it must not be drawn.
  - Rim at (3.2, -2.2, 0): colour #a855f7, edge lengths 2.0 (x), 2.0 (y) and 5.0 (z).
Nothing special has to be programmed for the clipping: it is what the camera's near and far planes do to ordinary solid boxes. As usual for solid surfaces, only the outside of a box is drawn (a face seen from behind is not drawn), so where a near or far plane cuts a box the part that is cut off simply is not there and the box is not filled in.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Mid, Demo.Slab, Demo.Far, Demo.Behind, Demo.Ghost, Demo.Rim

# Task: A white ball and floor lit by a red and a blue point light and a tinted ambient light

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #0a0a0f.
- One camera at (0, 3, 9) looking at the point (0, 0.5, 0), with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.8 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- Both solids use a physically based material of the metallic-roughness kind, non-metallic (metalness 0), so they show a diffuse colour and a weak specular highlight:
  - A sphere named Ball centred at (0, 1, 0), radius 1.0, base colour #f3f4f6, roughness 0.7.
  - A flat square named Floor, 12 x 12 units, one-sided, facing up (+Y), lying in the plane y = 0 and centred on the origin, base colour #e5e7eb, roughness 0.9.
- Two point lights, each shining equally in all directions with no range limit, and each with an illumination that falls off with the inverse square of the distance from the lamp. Each is calibrated so that, if it were white, a perfectly matte (Lambertian) white surface that is 3 units from it and whose normal points straight at it would render as exactly white; a surface at an angle to the light receives proportionally less (the cosine of the angle). Their colours multiply that illumination:
  - LampLeft at (-3, 2.5, 2), light colour #ff3030.
  - LampRight at (3, 2.5, 2), light colour #3050ff.
- A uniform ambient light of colour #6070a0 at 10% of the strength a white light of that calibration would have: it adds to every surface, regardless of its orientation, 10% of the surface's own diffuse colour multiplied by the ambient colour.
The light colours and the surface colours are given as sRGB hex colours, and the lighting arithmetic is done on linear values. There are no shadows and no tone mapping: values above full brightness are simply clipped. The expected pixels were computed with the standard model (Lambertian diffuse plus a GGX specular term with Schlick Fresnel) and are checked with a tolerance of 6 per colour channel, which covers the small differences between implementations of that model (the shading of a tessellated sphere, rounding).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.LampLeft, Demo.LampRight, Demo.Floor, Demo.Ball

messages.content:
# Task: A white ball and floor lit by a red and a blue point light and a tinted ambient light

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #0a0a0f.
- One camera at (0, 3, 9) looking at the point (0, 0.5, 0), with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.8 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- Both solids use a physically based material of the metallic-roughness kind, non-metallic (metalness 0), so they show a diffuse colour and a weak specular highlight:
  - A sphere named Ball centred at (0, 1, 0), radius 1.0, base colour #f3f4f6, roughness 0.7.
  - A flat square named Floor, 12 x 12 units, one-sided, facing up (+Y), lying in the plane y = 0 and centred on the origin, base colour #e5e7eb, roughness 0.9.
- Two point lights, each shining equally in all directions with no range limit, and each with an illumination that falls off with the inverse square of the distance from the lamp. Each is calibrated so that, if it were white, a perfectly matte (Lambertian) white surface that is 3 units from it and whose normal points straight at it would render as exactly white; a surface at an angle to the light receives proportionally less (the cosine of the angle). Their colours multiply that illumination:
  - LampLeft at (-3, 2.5, 2), light colour #ff3030.
  - LampRight at (3, 2.5, 2), light colour #3050ff.
- A uniform ambient light of colour #6070a0 at 10% of the strength a white light of that calibration would have: it adds to every surface, regardless of its orientation, 10% of the surface's own diffuse colour multiplied by the ambient colour.
The light colours and the surface colours are given as sRGB hex colours, and the lighting arithmetic is done on linear values. There are no shadows and no tone mapping: values above full brightness are simply clipped. The expected pixels were computed with the standard model (Lambertian diffuse plus a GGX specular term with Schlick Fresnel) and are checked with a tolerance of 6 per colour channel, which covers the small differences between implementations of that model (the shading of a tessellated sphere, rounding).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.LampLeft, Demo.LampRight, Demo.Floor, Demo.Ball

messages.content:
# Task: A white ball and floor lit by a red and a blue point light and a tinted ambient light

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #0a0a0f.
- One camera at (0, 3, 9) looking at the point (0, 0.5, 0), with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.8 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- Both solids use a physically based material of the metallic-roughness kind, non-metallic (metalness 0), so they show a diffuse colour and a weak specular highlight:
  - A sphere named Ball centred at (0, 1, 0), radius 1.0, base colour #f3f4f6, roughness 0.7.
  - A flat square named Floor, 12 x 12 units, one-sided, facing up (+Y), lying in the plane y = 0 and centred on the origin, base colour #e5e7eb, roughness 0.9.
- Two point lights, each shining equally in all directions with no range limit, and each with an illumination that falls off with the inverse square of the distance from the lamp. Each is calibrated so that, if it were white, a perfectly matte (Lambertian) white surface that is 3 units from it and whose normal points straight at it would render as exactly white; a surface at an angle to the light receives proportionally less (the cosine of the angle). Their colours multiply that illumination:
  - LampLeft at (-3, 2.5, 2), light colour #ff3030.
  - LampRight at (3, 2.5, 2), light colour #3050ff.
- A uniform ambient light of colour #6070a0 at 10% of the strength a white light of that calibration would have: it adds to every surface, regardless of its orientation, 10% of the surface's own diffuse colour multiplied by the ambient colour.
The light colours and the surface colours are given as sRGB hex colours, and the lighting arithmetic is done on linear values. There are no shadows and no tone mapping: values above full brightness are simply clipped. The expected pixels were computed with the standard model (Lambertian diffuse plus a GGX specular term with Schlick Fresnel) and are checked with a tolerance of 6 per colour channel, which covers the small differences between implementations of that model (the shading of a tessellated sphere, rounding).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.LampLeft, Demo.LampRight, Demo.Floor, Demo.Ball

messages.content:
# Task: A white ball and floor lit by a red and a blue point light and a tinted ambient light

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #0a0a0f.
- One camera at (0, 3, 9) looking at the point (0, 0.5, 0), with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.8 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- Both solids use a physically based material of the metallic-roughness kind, non-metallic (metalness 0), so they show a diffuse colour and a weak specular highlight:
  - A sphere named Ball centred at (0, 1, 0), radius 1.0, base colour #f3f4f6, roughness 0.7.
  - A flat square named Floor, 12 x 12 units, one-sided, facing up (+Y), lying in the plane y = 0 and centred on the origin, base colour #e5e7eb, roughness 0.9.
- Two point lights, each shining equally in all directions with no range limit, and each with an illumination that falls off with the inverse square of the distance from the lamp. Each is calibrated so that, if it were white, a perfectly matte (Lambertian) white surface that is 3 units from it and whose normal points straight at it would render as exactly white; a surface at an angle to the light receives proportionally less (the cosine of the angle). Their colours multiply that illumination:
  - LampLeft at (-3, 2.5, 2), light colour #ff3030.
  - LampRight at (3, 2.5, 2), light colour #3050ff.
- A uniform ambient light of colour #6070a0 at 10% of the strength a white light of that calibration would have: it adds to every surface, regardless of its orientation, 10% of the surface's own diffuse colour multiplied by the ambient colour.
The light colours and the surface colours are given as sRGB hex colours, and the lighting arithmetic is done on linear values. There are no shadows and no tone mapping: values above full brightness are simply clipped. The expected pixels were computed with the standard model (Lambertian diffuse plus a GGX specular term with Schlick Fresnel) and are checked with a tolerance of 6 per colour channel, which covers the small differences between implementations of that model (the shading of a tessellated sphere, rounding).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.LampLeft, Demo.LampRight, Demo.Floor, Demo.Ball

# Task: Three floor squares showing a 4 x 4 picture: hard-edged, tiled and smoothed

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #1b2430.
- One camera at (0, 11, 3) looking at the point (0, 0, 0), with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.72 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- The project contains the image file assets/swatch.png (path relative to the project directory): a 4 x 4 pixel picture whose sixteen pixels all have different colours. Three flat squares, each 3.6 x 3.6 units, one-sided, facing up (+Y) and lying in the plane y = 0, show it. The squares are unlit: the colour seen at a point of a square is the picture's colour there and nothing else (no lights, no shading, no tone mapping). On every square the picture is upright and unmirrored when the floor is seen from above with the camera's side (+Z) at the bottom: the picture's top edge lies along the square's far edge (the edge with the smaller z) and its left edge along the edge with the smaller x.
  - Plain, centred at (-2, 0, -2): the picture once, covering the whole square. The picture is magnified with hard edges: every point shows the colour of exactly one picture pixel, with no smoothing.
  - Tiled, centred at (0, 0, 2): the picture repeated twice across and twice down (four copies in a 2 x 2 arrangement, each copy upright and unmirrored as described), also with hard edges.
  - Smooth, centred at (2, 0, -2): the picture once, covering the whole square, magnified smoothly: between the centres of the picture's pixels the colour is the bilinear interpolation of the four nearest pixels, and outside the outermost pixel centres it is the colour of the outermost pixel (the picture does not wrap around).
- The picture's colours are sRGB-encoded, like those of any ordinary PNG file: a hard-edged picture pixel #bc4020 appears on the screen as #bc4020, and the smoothing blends in linear light (the colours are decoded to linear values, blended, and encoded again), as the filtering of an sRGB image does on a GPU.
The expected pixels were computed with an independent model of the scene (rays through the pixel centres, the picture's colours, bilinear filtering in linear light) and are checked with a tolerance of 2 per colour channel (3 on Smooth, because GPU filtering has limited precision).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Plain, Demo.Tiled, Demo.Smooth

# Task: Three floor squares showing a 4 x 4 picture: hard-edged, tiled and smoothed

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #1b2430.
- One camera at (0, 11, 3) looking at the point (0, 0, 0), with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.72 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- The project contains the image file assets/swatch.png (path relative to the project directory): a 4 x 4 pixel picture whose sixteen pixels all have different colours. Three flat squares, each 3.6 x 3.6 units, one-sided, facing up (+Y) and lying in the plane y = 0, show it. The squares are unlit: the colour seen at a point of a square is the picture's colour there and nothing else (no lights, no shading, no tone mapping). On every square the picture is upright and unmirrored when the floor is seen from above with the camera's side (+Z) at the bottom: the picture's top edge lies along the square's far edge (the edge with the smaller z) and its left edge along the edge with the smaller x.
  - Plain, centred at (-2, 0, -2): the picture once, covering the whole square. The picture is magnified with hard edges: every point shows the colour of exactly one picture pixel, with no smoothing.
  - Tiled, centred at (0, 0, 2): the picture repeated twice across and twice down (four copies in a 2 x 2 arrangement, each copy upright and unmirrored as described), also with hard edges.
  - Smooth, centred at (2, 0, -2): the picture once, covering the whole square, magnified smoothly: between the centres of the picture's pixels the colour is the bilinear interpolation of the four nearest pixels, and outside the outermost pixel centres it is the colour of the outermost pixel (the picture does not wrap around).
- The picture's colours are sRGB-encoded, like those of any ordinary PNG file: a hard-edged picture pixel #bc4020 appears on the screen as #bc4020, and the smoothing blends in linear light (the colours are decoded to linear values, blended, and encoded again), as the filtering of an sRGB image does on a GPU.
The expected pixels were computed with an independent model of the scene (rays through the pixel centres, the picture's colours, bilinear filtering in linear light) and are checked with a tolerance of 2 per colour channel (3 on Smooth, because GPU filtering has limited precision).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Plain, Demo.Tiled, Demo.Smooth

messages.content:
# Task: Three floor squares showing a 4 x 4 picture: hard-edged, tiled and smoothed

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #1b2430.
- One camera at (0, 11, 3) looking at the point (0, 0, 0), with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.72 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- The project contains the image file assets/swatch.png (path relative to the project directory): a 4 x 4 pixel picture whose sixteen pixels all have different colours. Three flat squares, each 3.6 x 3.6 units, one-sided, facing up (+Y) and lying in the plane y = 0, show it. The squares are unlit: the colour seen at a point of a square is the picture's colour there and nothing else (no lights, no shading, no tone mapping). On every square the picture is upright and unmirrored when the floor is seen from above with the camera's side (+Z) at the bottom: the picture's top edge lies along the square's far edge (the edge with the smaller z) and its left edge along the edge with the smaller x.
  - Plain, centred at (-2, 0, -2): the picture once, covering the whole square. The picture is magnified with hard edges: every point shows the colour of exactly one picture pixel, with no smoothing.
  - Tiled, centred at (0, 0, 2): the picture repeated twice across and twice down (four copies in a 2 x 2 arrangement, each copy upright and unmirrored as described), also with hard edges.
  - Smooth, centred at (2, 0, -2): the picture once, covering the whole square, magnified smoothly: between the centres of the picture's pixels the colour is the bilinear interpolation of the four nearest pixels, and outside the outermost pixel centres it is the colour of the outermost pixel (the picture does not wrap around).
- The picture's colours are sRGB-encoded, like those of any ordinary PNG file: a hard-edged picture pixel #bc4020 appears on the screen as #bc4020, and the smoothing blends in linear light (the colours are decoded to linear values, blended, and encoded again), as the filtering of an sRGB image does on a GPU.
The expected pixels were computed with an independent model of the scene (rays through the pixel centres, the picture's colours, bilinear filtering in linear light) and are checked with a tolerance of 2 per colour channel (3 on Smooth, because GPU filtering has limited precision).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Plain, Demo.Tiled, Demo.Smooth

messages.content:
# Task: Three floor squares showing a 4 x 4 picture: hard-edged, tiled and smoothed

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #1b2430.
- One camera at (0, 11, 3) looking at the point (0, 0, 0), with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.72 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- The project contains the image file assets/swatch.png (path relative to the project directory): a 4 x 4 pixel picture whose sixteen pixels all have different colours. Three flat squares, each 3.6 x 3.6 units, one-sided, facing up (+Y) and lying in the plane y = 0, show it. The squares are unlit: the colour seen at a point of a square is the picture's colour there and nothing else (no lights, no shading, no tone mapping). On every square the picture is upright and unmirrored when the floor is seen from above with the camera's side (+Z) at the bottom: the picture's top edge lies along the square's far edge (the edge with the smaller z) and its left edge along the edge with the smaller x.
  - Plain, centred at (-2, 0, -2): the picture once, covering the whole square. The picture is magnified with hard edges: every point shows the colour of exactly one picture pixel, with no smoothing.
  - Tiled, centred at (0, 0, 2): the picture repeated twice across and twice down (four copies in a 2 x 2 arrangement, each copy upright and unmirrored as described), also with hard edges.
  - Smooth, centred at (2, 0, -2): the picture once, covering the whole square, magnified smoothly: between the centres of the picture's pixels the colour is the bilinear interpolation of the four nearest pixels, and outside the outermost pixel centres it is the colour of the outermost pixel (the picture does not wrap around).
- The picture's colours are sRGB-encoded, like those of any ordinary PNG file: a hard-edged picture pixel #bc4020 appears on the screen as #bc4020, and the smoothing blends in linear light (the colours are decoded to linear values, blended, and encoded again), as the filtering of an sRGB image does on a GPU.
The expected pixels were computed with an independent model of the scene (rays through the pixel centres, the picture's colours, bilinear filtering in linear light) and are checked with a tolerance of 2 per colour channel (3 on Smooth, because GPU filtering has limited precision).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Plain, Demo.Tiled, Demo.Smooth

# Task: Set the cube's colour from the host input tint

The scene Demo shows a cube named Cube drawn with a custom material named Flat whose colour is fixed at #808080.
Make the cube's colour settable from the host page through an input named tint, whose value is a colour string such as "#ff8800": the material gets a colour parameter that follows a scene state, and the host input writes that state. Until the host sets a value the cube stays #808080. The colour must change by updating a value only; the material and its shader are not replaced. Everything else stays as it is.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Cube, Flat

# Task: One host input drives the grey of two cubes

The scene Demo shows two cubes, Left at (-1.2, 0, 0) and Right at (1.2, 0, 0), each drawn with its own custom material named Shade. Shade is not lit: it draws a flat grey whose red, green and blue values in linear light are all 0.25 (shown on screen as the sRGB grey #898989).

Left shows the grey whose linear light value equals the level. Right shows the complementary grey, whose linear light value is 1 minus the level. Both cubes keep drawing with a Shade material, and a new level must change values only: no material or shader is replaced. Everything else stays as it is.

messages.content:
# Task: One host input drives the grey of two cubes

The scene Demo shows two cubes, Left at (-1.2, 0, 0) and Right at (1.2, 0, 0), each drawn with its own custom material named Shade. Shade is not lit: it draws a flat grey whose red, green and blue values in linear light are all 0.25 (shown on screen as the sRGB grey #898989).
Make the greys settable from the host page through an input named level, whose value is a number from 0 to 1. The input sets one shared value, the level, which is 0.25 until the host sets it. Left shows the grey whose linear light value equals the level. Right shows the complementary grey, whose linear light value is 1 minus the level. Both cubes keep drawing with a Shade material, and a new level must change values only: no material or shader is replaced. Everything else stays as it is.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Left, Demo.Right, Shade

# Task: One host input drives the grey of two cubes

The scene Demo shows two cubes, Left at (-1.2, 0, 0) and Right at (1.2, 0, 0), each drawn with its own custom material named Shade. Shade is not lit: it draws a flat grey whose red, green and blue values in linear light are all 0.25 (shown on screen as the sRGB grey #898989).
Make the greys settable from the host page through an input named level, whose value is a number from 0 to 1. The input sets one shared value, the level, which is 0.25 until the host sets it. Left shows the grey whose linear light value equals the level. Right shows the complementary grey, whose linear light value is 1 minus the level. Both cubes keep drawing with a Shade material, and a new level must change values only: no material or shader is replaced. Everything else stays as it is.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Left, Demo.Right, Shade

# Task: A panel whose colour sweeps with time, computed in a custom material

Build a scene named Demo that renders as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #202020.
- One camera at (0, 0, 6) looking at the origin, with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.9 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- A box named Panel at (0.4, 0, 0), 4 wide (x), 2 high (y) and 0.2 deep (z), drawn with a custom material named Sweep. The surface is not lit. Its colour is computed for every pixel from x, the x coordinate of the surface point in the box's own object space (in metres, so it runs from -2 to 2 across the panel wherever the panel stands), and from t, the elapsed time in seconds: let w = 0.5 + 0.5 * sin(0.8 * x + t); the colour is (1 - w) * A + w * B with A = #1a237e and B = #ffb300. The blend is done in linear light, on the two colours converted from sRGB to linear, and the result is displayed as it is.
- t is the elapsed time of the application: the sum of the durations of all the frames run so far, including the frame being drawn (after 16 frames of 0.0625 seconds each, t is 1). t must reach the material as a value that is updated every frame; the material and its shader are not replaced as time passes.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Panel, Sweep

messages.content:
# Task: A panel whose colour sweeps with time, computed in a custom material

Build a scene named Demo that renders as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #202020.
- One camera at (0, 0, 6) looking at the origin, with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.9 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- A box named Panel at (0.4, 0, 0), 4 wide (x), 2 high (y) and 0.2 deep (z), drawn with a custom material named Sweep. The surface is not lit. Its colour is computed for every pixel from x, the x coordinate of the surface point in the box's own object space (in metres, so it runs from -2 to 2 across the panel wherever the panel stands), and from t, the elapsed time in seconds: let w = 0.5 + 0.5 * sin(0.8 * x + t); the colour is (1 - w) * A + w * B with A = #1a237e and B = #ffb300. The blend is done in linear light, on the two colours converted from sRGB to linear, and the result is displayed as it is.
- t is the elapsed time of the application: the sum of the durations of all the frames run so far, including the frame being drawn (after 16 frames of 0.0625 seconds each, t is 1). t must reach the material as a value that is updated every frame; the material and its shader are not replaced as time passes.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Panel, Sweep

messages.content:
# Task: A charge counted on the CPU shows as the grey of a cube

The scene Demo shows a cube named Meter at the origin, drawn with a custom material named Gauge. Gauge is not lit: it draws a flat grey whose red, green and blue values in linear light all equal its parameter level. The level is 0 in the starter, so the cube is black.
Make the cube show a charge. The charge is a whole number that starts at 0. Each time Space is pressed the charge goes up by one, but never above 4; each time Backspace is pressed the charge goes down by one, but never below 0. Gauge's level is always the charge divided by 4, so the cube is black at charge 0 and white at charge 4. Only the transition of a key from up to down counts as a press: a key held down is one press. The charge reaches the material as a value that is updated; no material or shader is replaced. Everything else stays as it is.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Meter, Gauge
